Have Mental Health Difficulties Risen Alongside Global Social Media Use?

Author

Lincon Chopra

Code 
.indent-block-tab {
text-indent: 2em;
}

Introduction

In this report, I investigate whether heavier technology and social media use is associated with higher levels of mental health difficulties such as anxiety, stress, and depression. I use several survey data sets from Kaggle that measure screen time and social media usage, along with self-reported mental health indicators. With this I can test whether, people who spend more time on screens and social media report worse mental health. I combine and standardize the data sets, explore trends, and run statistical tests to see how strongly usage and mental health are linked.

Overarching Question

How is social media usage associated with indicators of anxiety, depression, and attention difficulties among young adults worldwide?

Specific Question

Have mental health difficulties risen alongside global social media use?

Data Acquisition

I pulled all data directly from the Kaggle API instead of downloading the files manually. I used the official Kaggle command line to setup the downloads. Each dataset is stored in a separate folder under data/, and the code checks whether a CSV already exists before downloading again, preventing multiple downloads.

The three datasets I use are: Tech Use and Stress Wellness, Tech Gadget Usage and Mental Wellbeing, and Students’ Social Media Addictions.

check_kaggle_cli <- function() {
  # Try running `kaggle --version` and check exit status
  status <- system("kaggle --version", ignore.stdout = TRUE, ignore.stderr = TRUE)
  if (status != 0) {
    stop(
      "Kaggle CLI not found or not working.\n",
      "Install it with `pip install kaggle`,\n",
      "place your kaggle.json in ~/.kaggle/, and\n",
      "make sure `kaggle` is on your PATH."
    )
  }
}

# Run the check once
check_kaggle_cli()


# Helper: download Kaggle dataset


download_kaggle_dataset <- function(dataset, out_dir) {
  # dataset: "owner_slug/dataset_slug"
  # out_dir: directory for the dataset (e.g. "data/tech_use_stress")
  
  # Create directory if it doesn't exist
  if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) {
    dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)
  }
  
  # If there is already at least one CSV in out_dir, skip download
  existing_csv <- list.files(out_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
  if (length(existing_csv) > 0) {
    message("Found existing CSV in ", out_dir, " – skipping Kaggle download.")
    return(invisible(existing_csv))
  }
  
  # Build the Kaggle CLI command
  cmd <- sprintf(
    "kaggle datasets download -d %s -p %s --unzip",
    dataset,
    out_dir
  )
  
  message("Running: ", cmd)
  status <- system(cmd)
  
  if (status != 0) {
    stop(
      "Kaggle download failed for ", dataset, ".\n",
      "Check that the dataset name is correct and Kaggle CLI works.\n",
      "Command attempted: ", cmd
    )
  }
  
  # Return list of CSV files after download
  list.files(out_dir, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
}

# Helper: read a single CSV from each directory


read_single_csv <- function(dir_path) {
  csv_files <- list.files(dir_path, pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
  if (length(csv_files) == 0) {
    stop("No CSV files found in ", dir_path, ". Did the Kaggle download work?")
  }
  readr::read_csv(csv_files[1], show_col_types = FALSE)
}

tech_use_stress   <- read_single_csv("data/tech_use_stress")
gadget_mental     <- read_single_csv("data/gadget_mental_wellbeing")
social_media_rel  <- read_single_csv("data/social_media_relationships")

Data Cleaning

I clean the data by handling missing values, renaming variables, and ensuring that usage and mental health measures are normalized. I then combined all of the data sets into one table for analysis. This lets me analyze all surveyed data together while still being able to see where it originated from.

mh_scales <- mh_wide |>
  summarise(
    mean_anx = mean(anxiety_score,    na.rm = TRUE),

    mean_str = mean(stress_score,     na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_str   = sd(stress_score,       na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_dep = mean(depression_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_dep   = sd(depression_score,   na.rm = TRUE)

Analysis and Visualizations

Using the cleaned data set, I compute summary statistics and correlations between technology/social media use and mental health scores. I then created four visualizations which help visualize whether higher usage is associated with worse mental health outcomes in the data.

Code 
mh_usage <- mh_wide |>
  mutate(
    # Social media usage groups based on hours
    usage_group = case_when(
      social_media_hours < 2 ~ "low",
      social_media_hours < 4 ~ "medium",
      TRUE                   ~ "high"
    ),
    usage_group = factor(usage_group, levels = c("low", "medium", "high")),
    
    # Standardized (z) scores for each mental health dimension
    z_anxiety = (anxiety_score    - mh_scales$mean_anx) / mh_scales$sd_anx,
    z_stress  = (stress_score     - mh_scales$mean_str) / mh_scales$sd_str,
    z_dep     = (depression_score - mh_scales$mean_dep) / mh_scales$sd_dep,
    
    # Composite normalized mental health difficulty index:
    # average of available z-scores
    mh_z = rowMeans(
      cbind(z_anxiety, z_stress, z_dep),
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    mh_z = ifelse(is.nan(mh_z), NA_real_, mh_z)
  )

Code 
# Compute correlation between screen time and anxiety 
cor_anx <- mh_usage |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    r = cor(screen_time_hours, anxiety_score, use = "complete.obs")
  ) |>
  dplyr::pull(r)

# Base ggplot: scatter + regression line 
base_screen_anx <- mh_usage |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(screen_time_hours), !is.na(anxiety_score)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = screen_time_hours, y = anxiety_score, color = usage_group)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1.8) +
  geom_smooth(
    method    = "lm",
    se        = TRUE,
    color     = "black",
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "plasma", end = 0.9) +
  labs(
    title    = "Screen Time and Anxiety",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Correlation between screen time and anxiety: r ≈ ",
      round(cor_anx, 2)
    ),
    x        = "Daily screen time (hours)",
    y        = "Anxiety score",
    color    = "Usage group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle    = element_text(size = 11, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    legend.position  = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

# marginal density plots 
p_screen_anx_marginal <- ggMarginal(
  base_screen_anx,
  type      = "density",  
  groupFill = TRUE,       # color margins by usage_group
  alpha     = 0.5
)

Conclusion

My specific question stated: have mental health difficulties risen alongside global social media use? To answer this, I combined three different Kaggle data sets with 6705 total respondents. On average, people in this dataset use screens about 5.2 hours per day and social media about 3.3 hours per day. Their average anxiety score is around 8.3.

The results are pretty clear. The scatterplots of screen time vs. anxiety and social media hours vs. depression both slope upward meaning heavier users tend to have higher mental health difficulty scores. The correlation between social media hours and anxiety is about 0.59, with a p-value of 0, which shows that this relationship isn’t just random. For depression, the correlation is smaller but still positive, so the trend is similar.

When I group people into low, medium, and high social media users, the same trend appears. The low use group has an average anxiety score of about 2.5, the medium group is around 6.9, and the high use group is up at roughly 11.5. There are plenty of people in each group, so these averages aren’t being driven by just a few outliers.

The two-sample t-test comparing anxiety in high vs. low social media users also supports the current evidence. The estimated difference in mean anxiety is about 9.08 points, with a 95% confidence interval from 8.86 to 9.29 and a p-value of 0. This tells us that high social media users are more anxious on average than low users.

My final conclusion is: in these three data sets, more social media use goes hand-in-hand with more mental health difficulties. This directly supports our overarching question: “How is social media usage associated with indicators of anxiety, depression, and attention difficulties among young adults worldwide?” and our specific question; by showing a clear, consistent link between heavier use and worse anxiety/depression outcomes.
